clue.text: Pnde just a novel denomination

definitions.note: the name of a novel, so it names the book's title

parts.note: the scan misprints the word pride here; vanity is excessive pride in oneself
just and fair both mean even-handed

explanation.surface: Someone takes pride in a new name for a religious denomination.
explanation.walkthrough: The scanned first word 'Pnde' is a misprint of 'Pride'. 'Denomination' suggests a church; here it means a name, and 'novel' is a book, not 'new'.
explanation.definitionFit: Vanity Fair is the title of Thackeray's famous Victorian novel, so it is literally the naming of a book.

clue.text: Sun gave out — invisible by day

indicators.note: letters that are out are put out of place, so their order is broken up

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
no letters: it extends the definition, since a far-off sun is a star seen only at night

explanation.surface: The sun gave out its light and then vanished by day.
explanation.walkthrough: The closing words 'invisible by day' extend the definition: a distant sun is a star, seen only at night.
explanation.definitionFit: Vega is a bright star in the constellation Lyra, and any star is a distant sun.

clue.text: Time the same here and in Australia

indicators.text: the same here and in Australia
indicators.note: Australia is down under, upside down in a down entry, so the word must read the same either way up

parts.note: midday, a time of day

explanation.surface: A remark that the clock shows the same hour in Britain and Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer, turning it over for the land down under reads it bottom to top, and this word survives unchanged.
explanation.definitionFit: Twelve o'clock in the middle of the day is a specific hour, so it serves as a time.

clue.text: Rallying grounds where one may hold the advantage?

definitions.text: Rallying grounds where one may hold the advantage?

parts.note: surface reading: places where troops or supporters gather and rally

parts.words: where one may hold the advantage?
parts.note: setter's reading: rallies are exchanges of shots, and advantage is the score after deuce in that game

explanation.surface: A general picks rallying points where his side will have the upper hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennis is played on courts, rallies are its long exchanges, and 'advantage' is its scoring term after deuce.

clue.text: Sacked — report to follow

definitions.meaning: first meaning: dismissed from a job

definitions.note: describes a gun that has been shot, whose bang follows
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a gun discharged, its report, the bang, following

explanation.surface: An employee has been dismissed, and a written report will come later.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Report' looks like paperwork about the dismissal; it is the loud crack of a gun going off.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means dismissed from employment and also discharged, as a weapon whose bang then follows.

clue.text: No minster can be intimate

indicators.note: 'can be' says the letters could become something else when rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A claim that no cathedral can feel cosy or personal.
explanation.definitionFit: Innermost feelings are the most private and personal, which is what intimate describes.

clue.text: Gained point of no return

parts.note: surface reading: the stage past which turning back is impossible
setter's reading: in tennis a serve the opponent cannot return wins a point outright

explanation.surface: Someone reached the moment beyond which there is no going back.
explanation.definitionFit: A tennis player who serves an untouchable ball wins the point without any return being made.

clue.text: A bosom friend — one in study by fine poet

indicators.note: 'one in' places the single letter inside the pair of pieces that follow

parts.note: to con is to study or learn by heart
F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencils
the Roman numeral for one
Dante Alighieri, the Italian poet

explanation.surface: A close friend sits in a study beside a talented poet.
explanation.walkthrough: The numeral for one sits between F and the Italian poet, and CON stands next to that group.
explanation.definitionFit: A confidante is a trusted woman to whom secrets are told, exactly a bosom friend.

clue.text: Country type lacking self-control

parts.note: surface reading: a kind of person with no restraint, a rustic sort
setter's reading: a kind of territory that does not govern itself but is ruled by another state

explanation.surface: A rural character who cannot restrain themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country type' suggests a rustic person; it is a category of nation, and 'self-control' means self-government.
explanation.definitionFit: A colony or territory ruled from elsewhere, without its own sovereign government, is called by this word.

clue.text: Charge for landslide damage

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a yearly fee paid to a freeholder for the land a building stands on

definitions.note: read as earth that has been torn
definitions.meaning: second meaning, read literally: earth that has been torn apart

explanation.surface: A bill presented for repairing the havoc a landslide caused.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke reads the answer as earth that has been torn, while it is really a fee for land.
explanation.definitionFit: Leaseholders pay a yearly sum to the freeholder for the plot under their property, so it is a charge.

clue.text: Game cry as ace follows ace, perhaps

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a children's card game

definitions.text: cry as ace follows ace, perhaps
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the shout in that game when two matching cards are turned up one after another

explanation.surface: A shout raised at a card table when one ace lands on another.
explanation.definitionFit: Players call out the game's own name when two cards of equal rank appear consecutively, so the name is both pastime and shout.

clue.text: So mergers can be misinterpreted by dismal Jimmies

indicators.note: something misinterpreted is read the wrong way, so the letters are taken in a different order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Pessimists may twist the meaning of company mergers.
explanation.walkthrough: A dismal Jimmy is an informal name for a gloomy person who always expects the worst.
explanation.definitionFit: People who spread alarming rumours and predict disaster are gloomy pessimists, which is what dismal Jimmies are.

clue.text: Leading astray when married is by the way

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for married
taken as written
a direction is the way one goes

explanation.surface: Someone remarks, in passing, that marriage involves deception.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By the way' reads as the idiom 'incidentally', but 'by' only joins, and 'the way' is a route.
explanation.definitionFit: Sending someone the wrong way, or deliberately distracting them, is the act of leading astray.

clue.text: Boxing record holders?

parts.note: surface reading: champions who hold records in the ring
setter's reading: a fight or scrap plus the volumes that keep records, albums of cuttings

explanation.surface: A question about the title holders of the boxing world.
explanation.walkthrough: A scrap is a fight, so the hyphenated parts read as fight volumes, while the whole is an album of pasted cuttings.
explanation.definitionFit: These albums hold pasted clippings and souvenirs, keeping a record, and their first half is a word for a fight.

clue.text: Trade ideas for making things we need

indicators.note: making something out of material means reshaping it, so the letters are rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Exchanging ideas in order to produce the goods we require.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin plural means things desired or required, essentials that are wanted or lacking.

clue.text: Sign on staff for increasing output?

definitions.text: Sign on staff for increasing output?

parts.words: Sign on staff for increasing output?
parts.note: surface reading: hire more employees to raise production
setter's reading: a marking on a musical stave telling players to grow gradually louder

explanation.surface: A factory manager plans to recruit more workers to boost production.
explanation.walkthrough: A staff (or stave) is the set of five lines music is written on, and output here is volume of sound.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the musical instruction, often written as a widening hairpin, for a gradual rise in loudness.

clue.text: Knight going to ground — a narrow escape

parts.note: N is the chess notation for a knight
a fox earths when it goes to ground in its burrow

explanation.surface: A knight dives to the ground and narrowly escapes.
explanation.definitionFit: A close call, where disaster was only just avoided, is a common phrase for a narrow escape.

clue.text: Study English author

parts.note: to read a subject is to study it at university
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: An instruction to study an English writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'English author' looks like one phrase, but English gives a letter and only author is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Reade was a Victorian novelist, author of The Cloister and the Hearth.

clue.text: Finish in gold as farewell gesture

definitions.note: the word is a spoken farewell rather than a gesture

indicators.note: 'in' places the first piece inside the second

parts.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
to die is to come to an end

explanation.surface: Finishing a race in gold position as a way of signing off.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for goodbye is used in English as a formal farewell.

clue.text: The inevitable weapon

definitions.meaning: first meaning: following necessarily, bound to happen
second meaning: a gun that keeps firing while the trigger is held

explanation.surface: A gloomy reference to a weapon that cannot be avoided.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that happens as a matter of course is unavoidable, and a self-loading firearm goes by the same word.

clue.text: Descriptive of runner's view of the London marathon?

definitions.text: Descriptive of runner's view of the London marathon?

parts.words: Descriptive of runner's view of the London marathon?
parts.note: surface reading: the stunning sights along the route through London
setter's reading: what the race does to the runner's lungs, leaving them gasping

explanation.surface: Describing what a London marathon runner sees on the way round.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means stunning or spectacular, and literally describes something that robs you of air, as 26 miles does.

clue.text: Not out of the wood say

definitions.text: Not out of the wood say

parts.note: surface reading: still in danger, not yet out of the woods
setter's reading: 'say' makes the first word stand for its sound-alike, a knot, and this is a knot taken from timber

explanation.surface: Someone is warned they are not out of trouble yet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' marks 'Not' as standing for a sound-alike, a knot, the hard lump in a tree trunk.
explanation.definitionFit: This rare dialect word means a knot or knob on a tree, and it was also a wooden ball used in a northern English game.

clue.text: Sorcerers use a bit of imagination

indicators.note: a bit of a word is a run of its letters taken from inside it

parts.note: the second to fifth letters of the word

explanation.surface: Wizards rely on a little imagination.
explanation.definitionFit: The plural of magus means wise men or magicians, practitioners of magic and sorcery.

clue.text: The author of Household Management's finishing school?

indicators.note: the finishing part of a name is its end, so its front is dropped

parts.note: Mrs Beeton wrote the famous Victorian Book of Household Management

explanation.surface: Asking whether Mrs Beeton ran a finishing school for young ladies.
explanation.walkthrough: A finishing school teaches social graces to girls; here 'finishing' takes the last four letters of BEETON, giving the boys' school ETON.
explanation.definitionFit: Eton College near Windsor is England's best-known private boarding school for boys.

clue.text: Figure for eggs per pound

parts.note: ova is the Latin plural for eggs
L is the abbreviation for a pound, from libra

explanation.surface: The price of eggs per pound weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figure' suggests a price; it is a shape.
explanation.definitionFit: An egg-shaped outline is a geometric figure, rounded and longer than it is wide.

clue.text: Place holder has taken commission

definitions.note: describes the officer: one who holds a commission

parts.note: lieu is French for place, as in 'in lieu of'
a tenant holds land or property

explanation.surface: Whoever is keeping a seat has accepted a fee for doing so.
explanation.walkthrough: The rank literally means placeholder, a deputy standing in place of a superior.
explanation.definitionFit: This officer rank is conferred by a commission, so its holder is someone who has taken one.

clue.text: Pickwick swallows hard humbug

indicators.note: whatever swallows something takes it inside itself

parts.note: Samuel Pickwick is the hero of Dickens's Pickwick Papers
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Mr Pickwick gulps down a hard boiled sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: A humbug is a British striped peppermint sweet, which the surface uses; the definition is the other sense, a fraud.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean a fraud or pretence, something not genuine that deceives.

clue.text: An example of the best defence?

definitions.text: An example of the best defence?

parts.note: surface reading: a superb defensive line or legal case
setter's reading: the proverb says attack is the best form of defence

explanation.surface: A question about the finest defence anyone could mount.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb holds that attack is the best defence, and hostile attacking behaviour is this word.
